topComments.author: sigmoid10
topComments.text: Going directly for the logprobs is always icky when you use a chat model as base, because they are trained to write prose as output. So your "choice" tokens and thus their probabilities might get diluted in whatever else it wanted to say. If you have to do it in the same way as this post, at least add clear system instructions and a carefully worded beginning to the assistant output section of the prompt to lower the chances of it wandering off immediately. I've found that using structured outputs solves this problem much better. Instead of letting a model generate only "A", "B" or "C" and looking at the probs, have it directly generate "Legitimate", "Spam" or "Phishing" or any other pre-defined option from a set of multi-token sequences. Behind the scenes it boils down to something quite similar, but you're not running into the risk that the model actually wanted to say "A phishing attempt seems likely, so answer (C) is correct.", which would lead "A" to have the highest probability in the first token. You can even use a reasoning budget this way either via inherent reasoning or a free-form part preceding the remaining output structure. You can also have it assign probabilities (either in words or numbers) using more complex output structures, but I would not rely on them much more than the token logprobs (they can still be quite good though).

stories.summary: This parody article demonstrates how to implement a simplified version of Jev, a hyped AI classification model, in just 25 lines of Python by loading a small language model and extracting probability distributions across predefined choices. The author humorously debunks the complexity surrounding Jev, showing that at its core it's simply a local inference tool that classifies prompts with multiple options and outputs probabilities—no synthetic data, reinforcement learning, or API calls needed.

# Summary

Jev is a useful zero-shot classification tool that provides typed decisions with probability scores without requiring training data, but the author argues its claimed "calibrated probabilities" cannot hold universally since calibration is data-distribution-specific—what's calibrated on TypeSafe's training data may be miscalibrated on your production data. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Is there a way to force GCC (or Clang?) to emit function bodies with a single exit point at the very end?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am porting a copy-and-patch JIT, which apparently used to build just fine with GCC 3, to a modern version of GCC. One problem I ran into is that in modern GCC, the template functions used by the JIT are no longer generated with a single exit point. Consider this (simplistic and completely unrealistic, but illustrative enough) example: extern void foo(void); extern _Noreturn void bar(void); int quux(int a) { if (a) { foo(); return 0; } bar(); } which results in assembly like this: quux: subq $8, %rsp testl %edi, %edi je .L7 call foo xorl %eax, %eax addq $8, %rsp ret .L7: call bar In this code, the ret instruction is placed in the middle of the function. This is a problem for the JIT, which wants to chop off the return instruction at the end of each template function and string their bodies together in the output buffer, expecting control flow to fall through seamlessly between them. What I need is an attribute or a compiler option which when enabled, guarantees that there is only a single return instruction at the very end of the function. Even if the code generator wants to place an early exit point in the middle of a function, it should emit a jump instruction to the return at the end of its code instead of placing a return instruction there directly. It should probably also disable emitting tail calls, unless the called function is marked non-returning. Is such a thing available, or am I resigned to post-processing the assembly and hoping for the best? (Has a feature request for this ever been submitted somewhere at least?)

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How should I publish multiple Redis Stream events concurrently in TypeScript?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm building an event service in TypeScript that publishes events to a Redis Stream. For a single event, I currently have something like this: async publish(event: Event<EventStream.App>): Promise<string> { return this.redis.xAdd(this.stream, '*', { event: JSON.stringify(event), }); } I now want to add a bulk publishing method: async publishBulk( events: Event<EventStream.App>[], ): Promise<string[]> { // implementation } My first thought was to use Promise.all(): async publishBulk( events: Event<EventStream.App>[], ): Promise<string[]> { return Promise.all(events.map((event) => this.publish(event))); } This should allow the Redis commands to execute concurrently instead of waiting for each event to finish before publishing the next one. However, I'm concerned about using Promise.all() when the array contains a large number of events. For example, if there are several thousand events, this would potentially create thousands of concurrent Redis operations. What would be the recommended approach for implementing this? Specifically: Is Promise.all(events.map(...)) appropriate for a reasonably sized batch? Should I limit concurrency for larger batches? Would Redis pipelining or MULTI/EXEC be preferable for this use case? What would a production-friendly TypeScript implementation look like? I'm using TypeScript with a Redis client that supports XADD.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Does requests.Session pick up changes to the file contents of a provided cert?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: The requests library in Python allows to implement authentication using client certificates. To do so, you have to pass paths to a cert and key file on disk, and requests loads them at some point before making a request. # initial setup of the requests session session = requests.Session() # repeated requests, running in a background loop resp = session.post(url=..., data=..., cert=('/path/client.cert', '/path/client.key') I have two boundary conditions: I need to use a requests.Session() (because I actually use requests via opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http ; and The certificates I want to use will be short-lived, and a spire-agent external to my application will make sure that a valid certificate is written to the files.
